records.title: A game is a way into a database
records.description: Under the hood, a game is a set of records and rules for changing them. Playing is a way of working with that data.

records.title: The display is not the data
records.description: What a screen shows is a copy, drawn from the data now and then. The two can disagree.

records.title: Learn the relations, not the flashcards

records.title: Complexity and coupling
records.description: Perrow's two measures of a risky system: how unexpectedly its parts can interact, and how little slack there is between them.
records.source: Charles Perrow, "Complexity, Coupling, and Catastrophe," from Normal Accidents: Living with High-Risk Technologies (1984; 1999 edition), syllabus Nov 16 (paraphrase)
records.text:
In Charles Perrow's terms, a system is **interactively complex** when its parts can affect each other in ways no one planned or can easily see, and **tightly coupled** when one step follows another with no time, slack or substitute in between. When a system is both, a small failure can spread faster than anyone can understand it. Perrow calls the accidents such systems produce "normal accidents": not freak events, but something the system's design makes inevitable sooner or later.

Source: Charles Perrow, "Complexity, Coupling, and Catastrophe," a chapter of *Normal Accidents: Living with High-Risk Technologies* (1984), assigned for November 16. This card is a paraphrase.

records.description: Hasan: data multiplying beyond what institutions can manage
records.text:
- Hasan: data multiplying beyond what institutions can manage

**Hasan's term for digitization's overshoot: data multiplying and circulating beyond what institutions can manage, without the control or service it promised.**

## In plain terms

Relational databases made data easy to copy, combine, query, and move. Hasan argues that in Indian government this produced more data, more copies, and more interfaces, but not better knowledge or better service. Leaks, duplicate records, and errors multiplied along with the records, and part of the work of containing them fell on citizens.

For database design, excess raises questions about copies and authority: when versions of a record circulate, which one is the [source of truth](single-source-of-truth.md), and who pays when they disagree?

## In the readings

Hasan introduces excess as his vantage point at the start of the chapter (p. 122) and ends with bureaucrats in Karnataka who said that after land records went digital, they "know less" about the lands under their jurisdiction (p. 162).

records.title: Infrastructure
records.description: Star: "a fundamentally relational concept" (p. 380)
records.text:
- Star: "a fundamentally relational concept" (p. 380)

**Star's term for the systems in the background of work, defined as a relation to practice rather than a thing: one person's infrastructure is another's topic or obstacle.**

## In plain terms

Pipes, wires, standards, forms, and databases become infrastructure when the people using them take them for granted. Turn on a faucet and you use a vast water system without thinking about it; for the engineer who maintains it, the system is the job. A database is infrastructure for a Spotify listener and the daily object of work for the engineer who keeps it running.

Star lists the properties: infrastructure is embedded in other structures; transparent to use; has reach beyond one site or event; is learned as part of membership; links with conventions of practice; embodies standards; is built on an installed base; becomes visible upon breakdown; and is fixed in modular increments, never all at once. Each applies to databases. A schema is an installed base; a failed login makes the whole system visible.

Bowker's phrase "infrastructural inversion," which Star uses, names the move of bringing these backstage elements to the foreground.

## In the readings

Star: "One person's infrastructure is another's topic, or difficulty," and infrastructure is "a fundamentally relational concept" (p. 380). The properties are on pp. 381–382. Her teacher Anselm Strauss's aphorism "study the unstudied" (p. 379) is the method in short.

records.title: Invisible work
records.description: Star: the labor that keeps a system running but doesn't show up in it
records.text:
- Star: the labor that keeps a system running but doesn't show up in it

**Star's term for the labor that keeps a system running but doesn't appear in it: workarounds, corrections, and the adjustments that fill the gaps between what the system expects and what happens.**

## In plain terms

Every database depends on people who make the data fit: the clerk who reformats an address so the form will accept it, the operator who knows which records are duplicates, the applicant who invents a date because the field is required. None of that work appears in the final record, which looks clean because someone cleaned it. Star calls the real-time adjustments that complete a process *articulation work*.

Places to look for it: the [audit trail](audit-trail.md) (corrections and reversals), the "notes" and "other" fields, the workarounds people describe when asked how they use a system, and the gap between a form's categories and what people write in the margins.

## In the readings

Star, pp. 385–386: information systems can sit in a work process "like a rock in a stream," requiring workarounds, and can leave gaps that require "articulation work"; finding it can mean going "backstage." Hasan's landholders, running between offices to repair their own records, do invisible work of another kind (pp. 154–155).

records.title: Master narrative
records.description: Star: the single, unmarked point of view a system builds in
records.text:
- Star: the single, unmarked point of view a system builds in

**Star's term for the single, unmarked point of view a system builds in, treating one kind of life as normal and everything else as "other" or absent.**

## In plain terms

A form speaks from a presumed center. It assumes the person filling it in has a husband, a fixed address, a first and last name in the expected order. People who fit never notice. People who don't have to bend their lives to the boxes or go unrecorded. Star's method is to listen for this voice by starting from those it leaves out.

In a database, the master narrative lives in the [schema](schema.md): which entities exist, which attributes are required, which values the [controlled vocabulary](controlled-vocabulary.md) allows, what counts as "other." It's usually not deliberate, which is part of what makes it infrastructure.

## In the readings

Star, p. 384: many information systems employ "a single voice that does not problematize diversity"; her example is a medical history form with blanks for "maiden name" and "husband's name." Identifying the master narrative means "identifying first with that which has been made other" (p. 385).

records.title: Provisionality
records.description: Dourish: open-ended, "but only in the terms originally laid down in its structure"
records.text:
- Dourish: open-ended, "but only in the terms originally laid down in its structure"

**Dourish's word for the database's open-endedness, and its limit: content can be added and changed endlessly, but only within the structure laid down at the start.**

## In plain terms

A database feels infinitely open: new rows, new edits, new ways to search. That's the content. The structure (which tables, which columns, what a row is) is much harder to change, and it decides what any future content can say. Adding a million places costs nothing structurally. Adding "is this place wheelchair accessible?" is a [migration](schema-migration.md), and every existing place starts out unknown.

The takeaway for reading any database: ask what's cheap to change and what's expensive. The expensive parts are where the assumptions live.

## In the readings

Dourish (section "The Materialities of Relational Data"): "So the database is provisional, but only with limits; it is open-ended, but only in the terms originally laid down in its structure." He separates narrative and archival provisionality, which concern content, from the schema's resistance to change.

records.title: Slow violence
records.description: Nixon's term; Hasan applies it to repairing land records
records.text:
- Nixon's term; Hasan applies it to repairing land records

**Rob Nixon's term, which Hasan applies to data: harm that is gradual, dispersed, and hard to trace to its cause, like the long work of repairing a wrong record.**

## In plain terms

Not a crash or a spectacular failure, but months of office visits, lost days of work, fees to brokers, and waiting for a hearing, all to fix a mistake someone else made in a database. The harm is spread out in time and buried in ordinary bureaucracy, so it's hard to see as harm at all.

For database thinking, the point is that the cost of an error doesn't fall where the error was made. One mistyped value, or a status set to "dispute," can move the work of correction onto the person the record describes.

## In the readings

Hasan introduces the term early (pp. 133–134) and describes data repair as "circuitous low-grade suffering" (p. 153), citing the environmental humanities scholar Rob Nixon's *Slow Violence and the Environmentalism of the Poor* (2011). The Bhoomi land-records case (pp. 153–155) is his example.

records.title: Symbolic form
records.description: Manovich, after Panofsky: a form that is also a way of seeing the world
records.text:
- Manovich, after Panofsky: a form that is also a way of seeing the world

**Manovich's term, after the art historian Erwin Panofsky: a form that is also a way of seeing the world, as linear perspective was for the modern age.**

## In plain terms

Panofsky argued that Renaissance perspective wasn't only a drawing technique: it built a particular idea of space, and of the viewer's place in it, into every picture made with it. Manovich borrows the phrase to claim the database does the same for the computer age. It's a storage technology, but also a model of what a world is: a collection of items to be searched and recombined rather than a story to be followed.

For this workshop, the question is how far the claim reaches under the hood. Manovich works at the level of user experience. The technical choices in this glossary (tables or documents, folders or tags, what a row is) are where a "model of the world" gets built, one decision at a time.

## In the readings

Manovich, p. 81: following Panofsky's analysis of linear perspective as a "symbolic form," we may call the database "a new symbolic form of the computer age," "a new way to structure our experience" of ourselves and the world.

records.title: Vacant citizenship
records.description: Hasan's term for citizens whose claims wait while they repair their own data (p. 162)
records.text:
- Hasan's term for citizens whose claims wait while they repair their own data (p. 162)

**Hasan's term for the condition of citizens whose claims on the state are suspended while they repair their own data.**

## In plain terms

When a land record is wrong, the benefits and entitlements tied to that record stop until it's fixed, and fixing it becomes the landholder's job. For that period they are citizens on paper but can't use what citizenship should give them. Hasan describes this as a shift from "thick," substantive citizenship to "thin" citizenship.

In database terms: a record that's flagged, locked, or stuck in a dispute state stops working as the key to everything linked to it. Any system where benefits, access, or rights are looked up by record has this failure mode.

## In the readings

Hasan's conclusion: data excess forces citizen-beneficiaries to repair their data, "producing moments of vacant citizenship" (p. 162). The thick-to-thin shift is on p. 133; he calls repair "temporal vacuity, a state of limbo" (p. 153).

records.title: Visible upon breakdown
records.description: Working infrastructure is invisible. An outage, a hack or a storm makes it visible, for a while.
records.text:
> The normally invisible quality of working infrastructure becomes visible when it breaks: the server is down, the bridge washes out, there is a power blackout.
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure" (1999), p. 382

Star lists this as one of the properties of infrastructure: you mostly notice it when it fails. Brian Larkin (2013, a related reading) argues it's only half true: some infrastructure is built to be seen. See [the poetics of infrastructure](poetics-of-infrastructure.md). For recent breakdowns, see [/breakdowns](/breakdowns).

records.title: Ludonarrative dissonance
records.description: When what a game makes you do pulls against the story it tells.
records.text:
> a powerful dissonance between what it is about as a game, and what it is about as a story
>
> — Clint Hocking, "Ludonarrative Dissonance in Bioshock," *Click Nothing* (blog), October 7, 2007

Hocking named it writing about *BioShock*: the story argued one thing about self-interest while the mechanics rewarded another.

records.title: The ironies of automation
records.description: Automating the easy parts of a job can leave the person in charge with only the hard parts, and less practice at them.
records.source: Lisanne Bainbridge, "Ironies of Automation," Automatica 19:6 (1983): 775–779, p. 777; https://gwern.net/doc/sociology/technology/1983-bainbridge.pdf
records.text:
> By taking away the easy parts of his task, automation can make the difficult parts of the human operator's task more difficult
>
> — Lisanne Bainbridge, "Ironies of Automation," *Automatica* 19, no. 6 (1983), p. 777

Bainbridge was writing about industrial control rooms, long before AI agents. The operator watches a system that runs itself, and is expected to take over in exactly the moments it fails.

records.title: The moral crumple zone
records.description: When an automated system fails, the blame lands on the person nearest to it.
records.source: Madeleine Clare Elish, "Moral Crumple Zones" (2019), p. 40; https://estsjournal.org/index.php/ests/article/view/260
records.text:
> the moral crumple zone protects the integrity of the technological system, at the expense of the nearest human operator
>
> — Madeleine Clare Elish, "Moral Crumple Zones: Cautionary Tales in Human-Robot Interaction," *Engaging Science, Technology, and Society* 5 (2019), p. 40

A crumple zone is the part of a car built to absorb a crash. Elish's point is that people end up playing that part for automated systems: the system's reputation survives, the operator's doesn't.

records.title: Approval fatigue
records.description: Ask someone to approve enough things and approving stops being a decision.
records.source: CISA, "Implementing Number Matching in MFA Applications" (2022); https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/fact-sheet-implement-number-matching-in-mfa-applications-508c.pdf
records.text:
> until the user either approves the request by accident or out of annoyance
>
> — US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, "Implementing Number Matching in MFA Applications" (fact sheet, October 2022), on "MFA fatigue" attacks

Attackers send login prompts to someone's phone over and over until one gets approved.

records.title: The elemental tetrad
records.description: Every game is made of four kinds of thing: mechanics, story, aesthetics and technology. None ranks above the others.
records.source: Jesse Schell, The Art of Game Design (2008); Deck of Lenses, https://deck.artofgamedesign.com/
records.text:
> Are the four elements in harmony, reinforcing each other, and working together toward a common theme?
>
> — Jesse Schell, "The Elemental Tetrad," in his Deck of Lenses (from *The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lenses*, Morgan Kaufmann, 2008)

Schell's four: mechanics (the rules), story (what happens), aesthetics (how it looks, sounds and feels) and technology (what it runs on).

records.title: The paperclip maximizer
records.description: A thought experiment: an AI given one harmless goal and no limits could pursue it past every human interest.
records.source: Nick Bostrom, "Ethical Issues in Advanced Artificial Intelligence" (2003), section 2; https://nickbostrom.com/ethics/ai
records.text:
> It also seems perfectly possible to have a superintelligence whose sole goal is something completely arbitrary, such as to manufacture as many paperclips as possible, and who would resist with all its might any attempt to alter this goal.
>
> — Nick Bostrom, "Ethical Issues in Advanced Artificial Intelligence" (2003), section 2

Universal Paperclips (Frank Lantz, 2017) has you play this AI, one upgrade at a time. The game never states the argument; it has you carry it out.

records.title: The clicker as a thought experiment
records.description: A clicker game already asks you to make one arbitrary number go up; Universal Paperclips makes the player an AI doing just that.
records.source: Frank Lantz in Wired (October 21, 2017); see also Y Combinator interview, December 20, 2018
records.text:
> I thought, in a game like this, where the whole point is that you're in pursuit of maximizing a particular arbitrary quantity, it would be so funny if you were an AI and making paperclips. That game would design itself, I thought.
>
> — Frank Lantz, quoted by Adam Rogers, *Wired*, October 21, 2017

Lantz's point: clicker games already have you maximize one arbitrary number, so making the player an AI that maximizes paperclips took almost no change to the genre.

records.title: The poetics of infrastructure
records.description: Infrastructure isn't only technical: it is also a form that is built to be seen, to promise, to impress. Sometimes it is a spectacle, not invisible at all.
records.source: Larkin, "The Politics and Poetics of Infrastructure" (2013), pp. 329, 336
records.text:
> Focusing on the issue of form, or the poetics of infrastructure, allows us to understand how the political can be constituted through different means.
>
> — Brian Larkin, "The Politics and Poetics of Infrastructure," *Annual Review of Anthropology* 42 (2013), p. 329

Larkin argues against the idea that infrastructure is invisible until it breaks, the claim Star made famous:

> Thus many studies that begin by stating how infrastructures are invisible until they break down are fundamentally inaccurate. [...] Invisibility is certainly one aspect of infrastructure, but it is only one and at the extreme edge of a range of visibilities that move from unseen to grand spectacles and everything in between.
>
> — p. 336

His examples include slum residents in Mumbai who knew their water pipes by the names of the politicians who supplied them, and Suharto launching Indonesia's Palapa satellite with a button set in a ceremonial dagger. Larkin is a related reading, not on the syllabus.

records.title: Embeddedness
records.description: Infrastructure sits inside other structures, social arrangements and technologies, so people rarely see it as a separate thing.
records.source: Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," American Behavioral Scientist 43, no. 3 (1999): 377–391, p. 381.
records.text:
> Embeddedness. Infrastructure is sunk into and inside of other structures, social arrangements, and technologies. People do not necessarily distinguish the several coordinated aspects of infrastructure.
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," p. 381

Embeddedness is the first property of infrastructure on Star's list. Infrastructure is not a stand-alone object: it is sunk into other systems and into the ways people organize themselves. In the Worm Community study, the biologists did not tell apart the programs and parts of the software they used; they were simply inside it.

records.title: Transparency
records.description: Working infrastructure supports a task without having to be rebuilt or put together each time, so it goes unnoticed.
records.source: Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," American Behavioral Scientist 43, no. 3 (1999): 377–391, p. 381.
records.text:
> Transparency. Infrastructure is transparent to use, in the sense that it does not have to be reinvented each time or assembled for each task, but invisibly supports those tasks.
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," p. 381

> Thus, the step of using ftp made the system less than transparent for the biologists, and thus much less usable.
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," p. 381

For Star, infrastructure is transparent when people can use it without reassembling it for every task. Transparency depends on who is using it: downloading the Worm Community System by ftp was routine for computer scientists but new and hard for the biologists, and that one step made the system much less usable for them. Transparency is also what breakdown takes away.

records.title: Reach or scope
records.description: Infrastructure reaches beyond a single event or a single site, in space, in time, or both.
records.source: Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," American Behavioral Scientist 43, no. 3 (1999): 377–391, p. 381.
records.text:
> This may be either spatial or temporal—infrastructure has reach beyond a single event or one-site practice.
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," p. 381

Something counts as infrastructure only if it extends past one moment or one place. Star's example is temporal: her team scanned the biologists' quarterly newsletter into their system so that one of the community's long-term rhythms would carry over online.

records.title: Links with conventions of practice
records.description: Infrastructure and a community's habits shape each other.
records.source: Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," American Behavioral Scientist 43, no. 3 (1999): 377–391, p. 381.
records.text:
> Infrastructure both shapes and is shaped by the conventions of a community of practice (e.g., the ways that cycles of day-night work are affected by and affect electrical power rates and needs).
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," p. 381

> The practices of reporting quarterly via the newsletter could not be changed in the biologists' system—when we suggested continual update, it was soundly rejected as interfering with important conventions of practice.
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," p. 381

Infrastructure is not laid down on top of a community's practices; the two shape each other. Star's examples are day and night work cycles and electricity rates, and the QWERTY keyboard, whose limits passed from the typewriter to the computer keyboard and on to the design of computer furniture. The biologists rejected continual updates to their system because quarterly reporting through their newsletter was a convention they relied on.

records.title: Fixed in modular increments
records.description: Infrastructure is changed piece by piece and by negotiation, never all at once or from above, because nobody is really in charge of it.
records.source: Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," American Behavioral Scientist 43, no. 3 (1999): 377–391, p. 382.
records.text:
> Because infrastructure is big, layered, and complex, and because it means different things locally, it is never changed from above.
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," p. 382

> Nobody is really in charge of infrastructure.
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," p. 382

> There simply was no magic wand to be waved over the development effort.
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," p. 382

The last property on Star's list. Infrastructure is too big and layered, and means too many different things in different places, to be changed globally. Changes take time, negotiation and adjustment with the other systems they touch. When Star's team tried to get the system running in labs, they found lab computing tangled up with campus and hospital computing and with legacy systems.

records.title: Articulation work
records.description: The real-time adjustments people make to fill the gaps an information system leaves in their work.
records.source: Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," American Behavioral Scientist 43, no. 3 (1999): 377–391, p. 385.
records.text:
> They may sit in the middle of a work process like a rock in a stream, and require workarounds in order that interaction proceed around them. They also may leave gaps in work processes that require real-time adjustments, or articulation work, to complete the processes.
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," p. 385

> Finding the invisible work in information systems requires looking for these processes in the traces left behind by coders, designers, and users of systems
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," p. 385

Information systems never fit the work they serve exactly. Where a system blocks the flow of work, people build workarounds; where it leaves gaps, they make the running adjustments Star calls articulation work. This work is usually invisible, and finding it means going backstage and reading the traces left by a system's coders, designers and users.

records.title: Tiny barriers, magnified
records.description: A small extra step can stop people from using a system, because it disrupts the invisible work of fitting the system into everything else they are doing.
records.source: Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," American Behavioral Scientist 43, no. 3 (1999): 377–391, pp. 386–387.
records.text:
> seemingly trivial alterations in routine, or demands for action, will act to prevent them from using the system.
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," p. 386

> An extra keyboard stroke might as well be an extra 10 pushups.
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," p. 386

> The magnification we encountered in our studies of users concerns the disruption of the users' articulation work.
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," p. 387

Star calls this one of the paradoxes of infrastructure. In the Illinois Digital Library Project, an extra button, an extra link or even looking up from the screen was enough to keep people from using a system. Her explanation is not that users are irrational or rigid. Beside the visible work of keystrokes, users are weaving together their desks, routines and queues of tasks, and a small interruption to that weaving spreads through all of their work.

records.title: Heteropraxial and heteroglossial forms
records.description: A standard form only looks uniform: people fill it in differently, and its blanks carry many voices.
records.source: Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," American Behavioral Scientist 43, no. 3 (1999): 377–391, p. 385.
records.text:
> In studies we read of the actual practices of filling in death certificates, the distinctions made by the "designers" upstream did not match the ways that attending doctors saw the world.
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," p. 385

> We came to understand how the blanks on the forms were both heteropraxial (different practices according to region, local constraints, beliefs) and heteroglossial (inscribing different voices in the seemingly monotonous form).
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," p. 385

In their study of the International Classification of Diseases, Star and Bowker found that the categories drawn up by designers did not match how doctors saw the world when they filled in death certificates. The same blanks were filled in different ways depending on region, local constraints and beliefs (heteropraxial), and they recorded many different voices (heteroglossial). This is the other side of a master narrative: a form written in one voice is used in many.

records.title: Levels of reference (the problem of indicators)
records.description: Information infrastructure can be read as a made artifact, as a trace of activity, or as a picture of the world, and a study has to know which reading it is making.
records.source: Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," American Behavioral Scientist 43, no. 3 (1999): 377–391, pp. 387–388.
records.text:
> One of the difficulties in studying infrastructure is distinguishing different levels of reference in one's subject matter.
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," p. 387

> The relationship between e-mail and the larger sphere of lived activity cannot be presumed, but must be investigated.
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," p. 388

> A common example is the substitution of precision for validity in the creation of a system of indicators or categories.
>
> — Susan Leigh Star, "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," p. 388

Star names three ways to read information infrastructure: as a material artifact people made, where its effects matter and the truth of its content does not; as a trace or record of activity, such as transaction logs or a classification system read for the values built into it; or as a true representation of the world. The three overlap, but mixing them up leads analysis astray, since a log or an archive of e-mail is not the same as the lives it records. She also warns of a political tactic: instead of arguing the large question, take control of the indicators, trading validity for precision, as happened in the making of the DSM.

records.title: The interface to a database
records.description: Underneath, nearly every new media object is a database, and making a work means building an interface to it.
records.source: Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," Convergence 5, no. 2 (1999): 80–99, p. 86.
records.text:
> In general, creating a work in new media can be understood as the construction of an interface to a database.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 86

> With new media, the content of the work and the interface become separate.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 86

> The new media object consists of one or more interfaces to a database of multimedia material.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 86

For Manovich, most new media objects are databases behind the surface, whatever they look like. The interface may simply give access to the records, as a page of thumbnails or a search engine does, or turn them into a very different experience: a 3D city made of letters, a body to explore, virtual animals that respond to the user. Because content and interface are now separate, the same material can have many interfaces; a work with only one is the exception, closer to a traditional art object.

records.title: Data structures and algorithms: the computer's ontology
records.description: Programming divides the world into data structures and algorithms, and computer culture projects those two halves onto culture.
records.source: Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," Convergence 5, no. 2 (1999): 80–99, pp. 83–84.
records.text:
> What we encounter here is an example of the general principle of new media: the projection of the ontology of a computer onto culture itself.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 83

> Algorithms and data structures have a symbiotic relationship.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 84

> Together, data structures and algorithms are two halves of the ontology of the world according to a computer.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 84

Computer programming describes the world with two kinds of things: data structures (any object, from a city's population to a chair, modelled as data organised for search and retrieval) and algorithms (any task, reduced to a sequence of simple operations). The more complex the data structure, the simpler the algorithm can be, and the reverse. Manovich argues that computer culture projects these two halves onto culture: databases such as CD-ROMs and websites carry the data half, and computer games carry the algorithm half.

records.title: Data has to be generated
records.description: Data is not simply found lying around: people have to make, collect and organise it.
records.source: Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," Convergence 5, no. 2 (1999): 80–99, p. 84.
records.text:
> However, the passive/active distinction is not quite accurate since data does not just exist - it has to be generated.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 84

> Data creators have to collect data and to organise it, or create it from scratch.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 84

It is tempting to treat data as passive and algorithms as active. Manovich says the distinction does not hold, because data does not just exist. Someone has to write the texts, take the photographs, record the audio and video, or digitise existing media, and then collect and organise the results.

records.title: Reality → media → data → database
records.description: Manovich's name for the computer age's cultural routine: record the world, digitise it, then clean, organise and index it.
records.source: Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," Convergence 5, no. 2 (1999): 80–99, p. 85.
records.text:
> Once it is digitised, the data has to be cleaned up, organised, indexed. The computer age brought with it a new cultural algorithm : reality -> media -> data -> database.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 85

> Now the map has become larger than the territory.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 85

In the 1990s, once the computer became a universal media machine, societies went into what Manovich calls a digitising craze: books, tapes, photographs and recordings were fed into computers, then cleaned, organised and indexed. The web made data indexing a hobby or a job for millions, and big commercial sites became front ends to company databases. Rewriting Borges's story of a map as large as its territory, Manovich notes that the indexes can outnumber the data they index.

records.title: A collection, not a story
records.description: Because a website can always be added to, it never has to be finished, and what keeps growing is a collection rather than a story.
records.source: Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," Convergence 5, no. 2 (1999): 80–99, p. 82.
records.text:
> The sites always grow.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 82

> If new elements are being added over time, the result is a collection, not a story.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 82

As original HTML defined it, a web page is a list of separate elements, and adding one more is as easy as adding a line to a file. Websites are files that can always be edited, so they never have to be complete, and they rarely are. Manovich argues that this openness gives the web an anti-narrative logic: material that keeps changing can be collected, but it is hard to keep a coherent story running through it.

records.title: Narrative as a trajectory through a database
records.description: A narrative can be seen as one path through a database, and an interactive narrative as the sum of many paths, though a path alone is not yet a story.
records.source: Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," Convergence 5, no. 2 (1999): 80–99, p. 87.
records.text:
> An interactive narrative [...] can then be understood as the sum of multiple trajectories through a database.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 87

> However, if the user simply accesses different elements, one after another, in a usually random order, there is no reason to assume that these elements will form a narrative at all.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 87

Manovich redefines narrative in database terms: the reader of a narrative follows links between records that the creator set up. An interactive narrative (a hyper-narrative) is the sum of many such paths, and a traditional linear narrative is one path among them. But a path is not automatically a story. The author still has to control what the elements mean and how they connect, and a user clicking through records in any order is not thereby making a narrative.

records.title: Database is the unmarked term
records.description: In computer culture the database is the default form, and narrative is the special case that has to be built on top of it.
records.source: Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," Convergence 5, no. 2 (1999): 80–99, pp. 87–88.
records.text:
> In the database/narrative pair, database is the unmarked term.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 87

> More precisely, a database can support narrative, but there is nothing in the logic of the medium itself which would foster its generation.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," pp. 87–88

In a pair of opposed terms, the unmarked term is the ordinary default and the marked term is the exception. Manovich says database and narrative do not have equal status in computer culture: whether a new media object presents itself as a linear narrative, an interactive narrative or a database, underneath it is a database. That is why databases take up so much of new media, and why it is narrative's survival there that needs explaining.

records.title: Two competing imaginations
records.description: Database and narrative are two old, basic ways of making sense of the world, older than any medium, and they keep mixing.
records.source: Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," Convergence 5, no. 2 (1999): 80–99, p. 92.
records.text:
> Both have existed long before modern media.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 92

> Competing to make meaning out of the world, database and narrative produce endless hybrids.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 92

> Modern media is the new battlefield for the competition between database and narrative.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 92

Manovich declines to derive database and narrative from particular technologies; a book, after all, holds both photo albums and novels. He treats them as two competing imaginations: the ancient Greeks wrote Homer's epics and also encyclopedias, and Diderot wrote novels and ran the Encyclopédie. Pure cases are rare, since encyclopedias tell stories and many novels travel through an imaginary encyclopedia. In his sketch of modern media, photography favoured catalogues and lists, film favoured narrative, and digital storage favours the database again.

records.title: Database cinema
records.description: Film footage is a database and editing draws one path through it; some filmmakers, above all Vertov, work on that problem on purpose.
records.source: Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," Convergence 5, no. 2 (1999): 80–99, pp. 94–97.
records.text:
> For cinema already exists precisely at the intersection between database and narrative.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 94

> During editing the editor constructs a film narrative out of this database, creating a unique trajectory through the conceptual space of all possible films which could have been constructed.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," p. 94

> Man with a Movie Camera traverses its database in a particular order to construct an argument.
>
> — Lev Manovich, "Database as Symbolic Form," pp. 96–97

All the footage shot for a film is a database, and editing makes one path through it, so every filmmaker deals with database and narrative, though few do so deliberately. Manovich's examples are Peter Greenaway, who orders his films by numbers, alphabets and colours and spreads his databases across museums and whole cities, and Dziga Vertov, whose Man with a Movie Camera arranges a catalogue of city shots and film techniques into an argument about modern life. In Vertov's hands, Manovich says, the database becomes dynamic and subjective, and database and narrative merge into a new form.

records.title: Three senses of “database”
records.description: Dourish separates three things that get called a database: a collection of data, data organized by a common scheme, and the software that manages it.
records.source: Dourish, Paul. 2014. “No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology.” Computational Culture 4 (9 November 2014), section “Database.”
records.text:
> In summary, a (3) database management system implements (2) a database, which organizes (1) a collection of data.
>
> — Paul Dourish, "No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology," section “Database”

> Arranging data into a common format makes each data item amenable to a common set of operations – data items can be sorted, compared, collated, grouped, summarized, processed, transformed, and related because a common format is employed.
>
> — Paul Dourish, "No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology," section “Database”

In everyday speech any large pile of data is a database. In the technical sense, data becomes a database only when it is encoded and organized by a common scheme, so that every item can be handled by the same operations. The third sense is the database management system, software such as Oracle or MySQL. Dourish argues that the middle layer, the common data format, deserves the most attention, because it is where the choices about representing the world are made.

records.title: The ACID regime
records.description: Dourish's name for the mutually reinforcing system of relational data, strict transaction rules, hardware designed to run them, and benchmarks that measured them.
records.source: Dourish, Paul. 2014. “No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology.” Computational Culture 4 (9 November 2014), section “The Materialities of Relational Data Processing.”
records.text:
> Indeed, we could reasonably argue that the identification and definition of the ACID properties enabled, or at least fuelled, the development of the database field, or what we might call the ACID regime, which encompasses both the software and hardware developments that enable high transaction-throughput systems.
>
> — Paul Dourish, "No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology," section “The Materialities of Relational Data Processing”

> In the ACID regime we find at work highly entwined sociomaterial configurations.
>
> — Paul Dourish, "No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology," section “The Materialities of Relational Data Processing”

ACID names four guarantees for transactions: atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability. Dourish argues that they became more than rules, because IBM developed the relational model, built and rented the hardware, and supplied the benchmark by which database systems were judged, so the data model, the processing rules, the machines, and the measures of performance reinforced each other. Through Coase's idea of transaction costs, he links this to how organizations decide what to do in-house and what to outsource. Bank accounts are the regime's typical example.

records.title: Map-reduce
records.description: Google's programming model that splits a large task into many small independent tasks and then combines their results, which suits some problems well and others badly.
records.source: Dourish, Paul. 2014. “No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology.” Computational Culture 4 (9 November 2014), section “Shifting Materialities.”
records.text:
> For instance, counting up the number of barbers in a city can be easily decomposed by dividing the city into smaller regions, counting up barbers in each region in parallel and combining the results. Counting up the number of distinct roads, though, cannot be broken down the same way because roads will cross the boundaries of smaller regions; the decisions are not independent when the decomposition is spatial.
>
> — Paul Dourish, "No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology," section “Shifting Materialities”

“Map” breaks one large task into smaller tasks that run independently; “reduce” combines their results. Run on large clusters of ordinary computers instead of mainframes, it gives scale cheaply, but some tasks fit the model and others must be given up, and ACID-style consistency is hard to keep. Dourish treats it as the center of a second regime, with cloud services, loose consistency, and large informal collections such as Facebook's tagged photographs, set against the ACID regime's bank accounts.

records.title: Representational and effective form
records.description: A database is at once a notation for describing the world and an engineering object that makes computers do things, so its data model points both ways.
records.source: Dourish, Paul. 2014. “No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology.” Computational Culture 4 (9 November 2014), section “3. Multiplicity.” Second quotation: section “Conclusion.”
records.text:
> Fundamentally, the concern is that the database is both a representational form and an effective form; that is, databases provide a notation that people use to represent and reason about the world, which is simultaneously an engineering artifact that directs and structures the operation of computer systems. The data model points in two directions, which is precisely why the materialities matter.
>
> — Paul Dourish, "No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology," section “3. Multiplicity”

> The essence of computational representations is that they are effective, that is that they can be operated and operated upon so as to achieve particular results.
>
> — Paul Dourish, "No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology," section “Conclusion”

A choice about how to represent people, houses, or accounts is also a choice about how the machine stores, copies, and processes them. The reverse holds too: limits of hardware and software decide what can easily be represented. For Dourish this double nature is why the material details of databases matter for anyone interested in how they describe the world.

records.title: Associativity
records.description: How a database binds items together into collections: by matching values across rows and tables in the relational model, or by attaching values and links directly to objects in key-value systems.
records.source: Dourish, Paul. 2014. “No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology.” Computational Culture 4 (9 November 2014), section “2. Associativity.”
records.text:
> In relational systems, data objects are associated through patterns in data values.
>
> — Paul Dourish, "No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology," section “2. Associativity”

> Network structures map naturally and obviously onto the interaction patterns of web-based applications, including so-called social networking applications; they provide poor support, though, for analytic applications which need to summarize, sort, and aggregate information across data items.
>
> — Paul Dourish, "No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology," section “2. Associativity”

In a relational database, rows are gathered by their values: all managers earning over a certain salary, or two tables joined through a shared social security number to link names to license plates. In key-value systems, values belong directly to objects, and a value can point to another object, chaining objects into networks. Each way of associating makes some uses natural (social networks for chained objects, summaries and totals for tables) and others awkward.

records.title: Multiplicity
records.description: Dourish's term for a single piece of data existing as several copies in different places, and the work of acting on those copies coherently.
records.source: Dourish, Paul. 2014. “No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology.” Computational Culture 4 (9 November 2014), section “3. Multiplicity.”
records.text:
> What can be replicated, then, is not “the information about my bank account” or “the files relating to my book” – what is replicated are tables and relations, or whatever data objects make sense to the database, rather than to its users.
>
> — Paul Dourish, "No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology," section “3. Multiplicity”

> However, these material considerations ‘bleed through’ in interaction.
>
> — Paul Dourish, "No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology," section “3. Multiplicity”

Databases keep replicas so that data can be read quickly in many places, which helps most when data is read far more often than it is changed. What gets copied is decided by the data model, not by what users think of as one thing. Copies also let parts of a system work apart for a while, as when a laptop works offline and has to sync later. Replication is usually treated as a hidden internal detail, but Dourish argues that it shows up in what users experience.

records.title: Convergence
records.description: How a distributed database eventually resolves disagreements between its copies into one consistent state, and how the timing of that fits the timing of use.
records.source: Dourish, Paul. 2014. “No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology.” Computational Culture 4 (9 November 2014), section “4. Convergence.”
records.text:
> We can think of this as the stabilization or normalization of diversity and disagreement; databases that converge are those that eventually resolve partial inconsistencies into a consistent whole.
>
> — Paul Dourish, "No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology," section “4. Convergence”

> Further, the temporalities of database resolution mean that sometimes, from a user’s perspective, time flows backwards.
>
> — Paul Dourish, "No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology," section “4. Convergence”

Some inconsistency can be tolerated for a while (Dourish calls this bounded consistency): a bank needs account balances to be exact at once, but a misspelled name can wait until the end of the day. Traditional relational transactions never let inconsistency show outside the database, while looser systems expose more of the database's workings to the software around it. To converge, a system may have to undo actions a user believed were finished, so the question is not only how long convergence takes but whether it fits the rhythm of use, from tagged photos to a game drawn thirty times a second.

records.title: Easy or difficult, not possible or impossible
records.description: Dourish's test for a material property of a database: not what it makes possible or impossible, but what it makes easy, efficient, and natural, or hard, slow, and awkward.
records.source: Dourish, Paul. 2014. “No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology.” Computational Culture 4 (9 November 2014), section “2. Associativity.” Second quotation: section “Conclusion.”
records.text:
> Once again, as in other cases, the question is not whether particular operations are possible or impossible, but whether they are efficient or inefficient, easy or difficult, or natural or unnatural within particular programming frameworks.
>
> — Paul Dourish, "No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology," section “2. Associativity”

> First, it argues that material properties as those aspects of the fabric of information systems that constrain, shape, guide, and resist patterns of engagement and use.
>
> — Paul Dourish, "No SQL: The Shifting Materialities of Database Technology," section “Conclusion”

Almost anything can be done with almost any database if enough effort is spent. What differs is cost and naturalness, and those differences shape which systems get built and which questions get asked. Dourish's example from the section on granularity: if a house must be stored as a set of rooms, heating systems become easy to reason about and property rights become hard.

records.title: Techno-politics
records.description: Hasan's approach of tracing how political aims are built into technical systems and how technical systems in turn shape political questions.
records.source: Hasan, Nafis Aziz. 2022. “‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance.” In Overload, Creep, Excess: An Internet from India, edited by Nishant Shah, Ashish Rajadhyaksha, and Nafis Hasan, 121–162. Amsterdam: Institute of Network Cultures, pp. 122–127.
records.text:
> While emphasizing what I see as the tectonic effects of a single technology, I do not elide the political; indeed, I hope to provide something of a techno-political account of postliberalization in India: the ways in which political actions are embedded within technical forms and, conversely, technical objects shape political questions.
>
> — Nafis Aziz Hasan, "‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance," p. 124

> How does an algebraic relation used to arrange data change our relations with each other and with institutions?
>
> — Nafis Aziz Hasan, "‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance," p. 122

Hasan tells the story of India's economic liberalization through one technical object, the relational database management system (RDBMS), instead of treating technology as the plain result of political decisions. Offshored call centers depended on workers querying databases stored thousands of miles away, and the welfare program MGNREGA's social audits depended on officials querying an RDBMS. The same technology thus supports both the service economy and welfare, which is why he calls it central to how a whole population experiences government.

records.title: Digital governance as layers
records.description: Hasan's picture of digitized government as geological strata, with each new technology built on top of older paper and computer systems that keep working underneath at their own speeds.
records.source: Hasan, Nafis Aziz. 2022. “‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance.” In Overload, Creep, Excess: An Internet from India, edited by Nishant Shah, Ashish Rajadhyaksha, and Nafis Hasan, 121–162. Amsterdam: Institute of Network Cultures, p. 128.
records.text:
> This is a story that unfolds in a more or less stratigraphic manner.
>
> — Nafis Aziz Hasan, "‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance," p. 128

> Viewing the digitization of government in archaeological fashion, as a series of layers, offers a history of the present.
>
> — Nafis Aziz Hasan, "‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance," p. 128

The paper files of colonial-style bureaucracy had their own system; in the 1970s and 80s, engineers for India's Planning Commission abstracted that system and built databases on top of it; relational databases, graphical interfaces, and networks were then built on top of those. Each layer changed the organization and its flow of data, and each changes at a different speed. Reading the layers together, Hasan finds one thread: the choice of data management technology and the political possibilities that came with it.

records.title: Responsibilization
records.description: The shift in which citizens are made responsible for tasks of government, which Hasan finds in both the eager engineers who built databases and the farmers left to repair them.
records.source: Hasan, Nafis Aziz. 2022. “‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance.” In Overload, Creep, Excess: An Internet from India, edited by Nishant Shah, Ashish Rajadhyaksha, and Nafis Hasan, 121–162. Amsterdam: Institute of Network Cultures, pp. 131–133.
records.text:
> I do this by thinking about how technical configurations like RDBMS aid us in forming neoliberal subjects with particular characteristics, and how this in turn produces an altered terrain of citizenship: for instance, a shift from rights to responsibility by shifting older patterns of power by attributing new technical responsibilities to citizens.
>
> — Nafis Aziz Hasan, "‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance," p. 131

> For the kinds of labor of repair which I describe later in this essay are not bestowed onto citizens (like rights) but are instead tacitly elided by the state and its agents and shifted onto citizens.
>
> — Nafis Aziz Hasan, "‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance," p. 133

Citizenship is usually discussed as rights people can claim from the state; under neoliberal government it is also a set of responsibilities to govern oneself. Hasan describes two kinds. The first is entrepreneurial: engineers and consultants such as J. G. Krishnayya who took it upon themselves to improve government through systems design. The second is the unannounced burden placed on landholders whose digital records are wrong, which is not keeping one's own data current but cleaning up after the system.

records.title: The paper behind the database
records.description: Digitized land records in India still depend on paper verification, paper evidence, and paper procedures, so the database sits on top of a paper system rather than replacing it.
records.source: Hasan, Nafis Aziz. 2022. “‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance.” In Overload, Creep, Excess: An Internet from India, edited by Nishant Shah, Ashish Rajadhyaksha, and Nafis Hasan, 121–162. Amsterdam: Institute of Network Cultures, pp. 146–149.
records.text:
> A land records database is as much controlled by a paper economy as the physical records had once been.
>
> — Nafis Aziz Hasan, "‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance," p. 146

> The figures and numbers seen in the database are only the symbolic representation of an intricate process of record creation located between the field and the office.
>
> — Nafis Aziz Hasan, "‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance," p. 148

The first digital land records were typed from the old registers by contract workers and verified by the same village accountants whose record-keeping the database was supposed to move beyond, and verification took so long that the status of the land had often changed by the time a record was approved (p. 149). When a digital record is wrong, the landholder has to go back to paper: old documents, court orders, and files submitted by hand. The database mainly prints copies of records, while the authority behind each record still lives on paper.

records.title: Transactions versus records
records.description: Hasan's distinction between government services built on high volumes of transactions, which relational databases were designed for, and the slow work of recording and filing, which they were not.
records.source: Hasan, Nafis Aziz. 2022. “‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance.” In Overload, Creep, Excess: An Internet from India, edited by Nishant Shah, Ashish Rajadhyaksha, and Nafis Hasan, 121–162. Amsterdam: Institute of Network Cultures, pp. 146–148.
records.text:
> Land records, when digitized, are not transacted online in the same way that bank functions are, nor is there any ‘intelligence’ generated from their arrangement in an RDBMS upon which the government acts.
>
> — Nafis Aziz Hasan, "‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance," p. 146

> The printing of digitized records, its primary purpose, had been possible even with a file-based structure of storing data.
>
> — Nafis Aziz Hasan, "‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance," p. 148

Relational databases were sold to banks, stock exchanges, and companies with many transactions in many places, and the railway ticketing system is the government example that fits. Land records are rarely transacted, and no analysis is run on them; the aims of creating a land market or analyzing land use were never attempted. Hasan argues that adopting the technology where it was not needed brought its risks of leaks, errors, and tampering without its promised benefits.

records.title: Easy access, easy change
records.description: The same openness that let relational databases be queried by non-specialists from many places also made their data easier to alter, so ease of access became a source of risk.
records.source: Hasan, Nafis Aziz. 2022. “‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance.” In Overload, Creep, Excess: An Internet from India, edited by Nishant Shah, Ashish Rajadhyaksha, and Nafis Hasan, 121–162. Amsterdam: Institute of Network Cultures, pp. 127, 149–150.
records.text:
> Databasing by its very nature, and particularly RDBMS with its tables and easy format, provides the opportunity to access and change data.
>
> — Nafis Aziz Hasan, "‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance," p. 150

> The not-so-user-friendly file-based structure of the database is often more secure against intervention, an unintended consequence of design since a user needed to know the structure of the database in order to access it.
>
> — Nafis Aziz Hasan, "‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance," p. 150

Older systems were hard to use, and that difficulty protected them: to change data you had to know how it was stored. Relational databases removed that barrier, which was their great advantage, but anyone who reached the tables could change them. In Karnataka's land records, typing an asterisk into one column created a new, legitimate-looking record that an operator used to take out loans in a farmer's name (p. 149), and government land was transferred to a private individual by someone who logged in and changed the database (p. 150).

records.title: The central data bank
records.description: The 1970s plan by India's Planning Commission to gather government data into one central computerized data bank, and the lasting question it raised of where data should live and who should control it.
records.source: Hasan, Nafis Aziz. 2022. “‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance.” In Overload, Creep, Excess: An Internet from India, edited by Nishant Shah, Ashish Rajadhyaksha, and Nafis Hasan, 121–162. Amsterdam: Institute of Network Cultures, pp. 135–140.
records.text:
> The alternative, which is being followed now, is to construct a large central data bank administratively in one Division in the hope others will use it. Won’t happen! People want to control the information they use themselves.
>
> — J. G. Krishnayya, Letter to Raj Krishna of the Planning Commission, quoted in Hasan, ‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance, p. 136

> This was the problem of the location of data that the Commission was now aiming to centralize into a data bank.
>
> — Nafis Aziz Hasan, "‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance," p. 135

The management consultant J. G. Krishnayya argued that the government's departments should be linked into a network instead, and his magazine listed the costs of centralizing: longer delays, more errors, lost context, misleading aggregation, and power concentrated at the center (p. 137). The data bank struggled because departments would not digitize in its formats, and even when running it produced “only a trickle of data” (p. 140). Hasan treats the location and control of data as a problem that has followed Indian e-governance ever since.

records.title: Data localization
records.description: The policy of requiring data to be stored inside a country's borders, which Hasan reads as an attempt to secure data by stopping its movement instead of managing it.
records.source: Hasan, Nafis Aziz. 2022. “‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance.” In Overload, Creep, Excess: An Internet from India, edited by Nishant Shah, Ashish Rajadhyaksha, and Nafis Hasan, 121–162. Amsterdam: Institute of Network Cultures, pp. 130–131, 155–161.
records.text:
> The proposed Bill, on the other hand, appears to want to secure data by restricting mobility.
>
> — Nafis Aziz Hasan, "‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance," p. 131

> At the heart of data localization is the question of whether security is inherently related to the physical proximity of data.
>
> — Nafis Aziz Hasan, "‘Slow Violence’ and Vacant Citizenship: The Excesses of India’s Digital Governance," p. 156

India's proposed Personal Data Protection Bill would require personal data to be stored within the country. Hasan contrasts this with the state's earlier security efforts, such as a 1980 committee on securing communication lines, audit logs, third-party audits, and national IT audits, which all tried to keep data moving while limiting risk. Localization returns to an older picture of data as fixed in place, like records in a register; Hasan says he is arguing neither for nor against it (p. 156).

records.title: Filing as intellectual production
records.description: Following C. Wright Mills, Jones treats keeping and rearranging a filing system as a form of thinking, not just storage for thinking done elsewhere.
records.source: Jones, Graham M. 2021. “Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat.” In Experimenting with Ethnography: A Companion to Analysis, edited by Andrea Ballestero and Brit Ross Winthereik, 151–162. Durham, NC: Duke University Press, pp. 152–154.
records.text:
> The way we sort data, ephemera, notes to ourselves, clippings, articles, and so on into sets for storage and recall not only reflects our conceptual priorities at any given moment but shapes the course of future projects.
>
> — Graham M. Jones, "Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat," p. 152

> The maintenance of such a file is intellectual production
>
> — C. Wright Mills, “On Intellectual Craftsmanship,” quoted in Jones, Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat, p. 153

For Mills, the categories in a file grow and change, some dropped and others added, and the way they change is a record of a researcher's intellectual progress. Jones shows this in his own work: folders on ‘Isawa ritual, “Indigenous Illusionism,” and “Regimes of Enchantment” came together into an article whose interpretation, he writes, “had emerged quite naturally from my filing system” (p. 154).

records.title: Macro-level categorization
records.description: Sorting material at the level of whole folders, projects, and arguments, as opposed to coding data word by word or line by line.
records.source: Jones, Graham M. 2021. “Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat.” In Experimenting with Ethnography: A Companion to Analysis, edited by Andrea Ballestero and Brit Ross Winthereik, 151–162. Durham, NC: Duke University Press, pp. 151–152.
records.text:
> In what follows, however, I want to talk about categories on a macro rather than a micro level.
>
> — Graham M. Jones, "Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat," p. 152

> Finally, as we write up, we inevitably face a big, cumulative problem of categorization: What is our case study an example of?
>
> — Graham M. Jones, "Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat," p. 151

Ethnography, Jones says, begins and ends with categories: data is gathered by categories set in advance and by the categories of the people studied, then sorted into types afterward. Grounded theory and qualitative analysis software work at the micro level, coding text line by line. Jones is interested in the large containers, such as hanging files, folders, and writing projects, and how they are arranged, up to the largest category of all: what the whole case is an example of.

records.title: The logic of combination
records.description: Mills's phrase for how rearranging a filing system brings notes on different topics together and produces ideas no one planned.
records.source: Jones, Graham M. 2021. “Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat.” In Experimenting with Ethnography: A Companion to Analysis, edited by Andrea Ballestero and Brit Ross Winthereik, 151–162. Durham, NC: Duke University Press, pp. 153, 156.
records.text:
> As you re-arrange a filing system, you often find that you are, as it were, loosening your imagination. Apparently this occurs by means of your attempt to combine various ideas and notes on different topics. It is a sort of logic of combination, and ‘chance’ sometimes plays a curiously large part in it
>
> — C. Wright Mills, “On Intellectual Craftsmanship,” quoted in Jones, Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat, p. 153

> Moving organizational units forward and backward or intercalating them in new ways is an exploration of conceptual order.
>
> — Graham M. Jones, "Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat," p. 153

Rearranging is a way of thinking: putting material side by side in new orders suggests connections, and chance helps. Jones prefers paper because reorganizing it is cheap and physical, with piles, sticky notes, and colored sheets standing in for files so the whole system's structure, overlaps, and gaps can be seen at once (p. 156). He calls this his artisanal, “slow-file” approach.

records.title: Headings can follow classification
records.description: Categories do not have to be named before sorting begins; material can be grouped first and the groups named afterward.
records.source: Jones, Graham M. 2021. “Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat.” In Experimenting with Ethnography: A Companion to Analysis, edited by Andrea Ballestero and Brit Ross Winthereik, 151–162. Durham, NC: Duke University Press, pp. 155–156.
records.text:
> You only need to produce a few words—headings—and then sort documents accordingly. Frankly, you don’t even need headings. They can follow rather than precede classification.
>
> — Graham M. Jones, "Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat," p. 156

> Also, it’s important to remember that anything can go into your files as long as it jogs some association.
>
> — Graham M. Jones, "Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat," p. 156

Sorting first and naming later lets the categories come from the material instead of being imposed on it. Jones gives an example from fieldwork: sorting hundreds of magicians' business cards by their images produced types that became a new line of research on how magicians present themselves (p. 155). He also recommends filing as a low-pressure way to keep working when writing stalls.

records.title: The inertia of the filing system
records.description: A filing system that has worked can lock in the shape of a project and stop a researcher from seeing other ways to organize the same material.
records.source: Jones, Graham M. 2021. “Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat.” In Experimenting with Ethnography: A Companion to Analysis, edited by Andrea Ballestero and Brit Ross Winthereik, 151–162. Durham, NC: Duke University Press, pp. 157–158.
records.text:
> My filing system, however, seemed oriented to the contours of a book that was never meant to be, with the ‘Isawa case study as one chapter, and other chapters devoted to various traditions of indigenous illusionism and histories of colonial contact.
>
> — Graham M. Jones, "Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat," p. 157

> Succumbing to the inertia of the filing system, I effectively gave up on the project and relegated all of the files to deep storage.
>
> — Graham M. Jones, "Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat," p. 157

After his first article, Jones's folders were shaped for a book of parallel chapters, and he could not find enough sources to fill the others. Five years later he reread the same files with fresh eyes, reorganized them around a new theme, analogy, and started a new hanging file, “Dangerous Doubles,” that brought together material previously scattered across separate files (pp. 157–158). The categories that help you find things also set what you expect to find, which is why the method ends in recategorizing.

records.title: Native categories
records.description: The categories used by the people being studied, which shape a researcher's record alongside the researcher's own theoretical categories.
records.source: Jones, Graham M. 2021. “Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat.” In Experimenting with Ethnography: A Companion to Analysis, edited by Andrea Ballestero and Brit Ross Winthereik, 151–162. Durham, NC: Duke University Press, pp. 151, 160–161.
records.text:
> We gather data according to preestablished categories of theoretical and comparative concern, and we also require that the way our subjects categorize salient features of their experience shape what we record.
>
> — Graham M. Jones, "Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat," p. 151

> In making a filing system you have probably already used native categories; now make sure you also include native categorization practices—for instance, recurrent analogies—as file headings.
>
> — Graham M. Jones, "Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat," p. 161

In anthropology, “native” means belonging to the people studied, as opposed to the outside analyst. Jones separates native categories (the kinds into which people sort things) from native categorization practices (how they sort: labels, concepts, metaphors, analogies), and he asks researchers to treat both as headings in their files.

records.title: Analogy as categorization
records.description: To draw an analogy is to put two things in one category while marking their differences, and Jones diagrams this as a base mapped onto a target to produce a concept.
records.source: Jones, Graham M. 2021. “Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat.” In Experimenting with Ethnography: A Companion to Analysis, edited by Andrea Ballestero and Brit Ross Winthereik, 151–162. Durham, NC: Duke University Press, pp. 158–159.
records.text:
> Positing a cross-cultural analogy is also a mode of categorization—in the case I was considering, one that framed French illusionism and ‘Isawa rituals as somehow examples of the same thing (“magic”) but with crucial differences.
>
> — Graham M. Jones, "Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat," p. 158

> culture consists in the way people draw analogies between different domains of their worlds.
>
> — Marilyn Strathern, Reproducing the Future (1992), quoted in Jones, Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat, p. 159

Following the psychologist Dedre Gentner, Jones describes analogy as mapping patterns from a familiar base domain onto an unfamiliar target domain, which yields an abstract concept; he draws it as a triangle with the base at lower left, the target at lower right, and the concept at the top. French writers mapped Western stage magic onto ‘Isawa ritual and produced the concept of “primitive magic,” an analogy Jones calls “inaccurate, tendentious, and racist” but culturally productive for claims of French superiority (p. 158).

records.title: Meta-analogy
records.description: An analogy between two groups' analogies, which Jones used to show how anthropologists and stage magicians together built the idea of a disenchanted modern West.
records.source: Jones, Graham M. 2021. “Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat.” In Experimenting with Ethnography: A Companion to Analysis, edited by Andrea Ballestero and Brit Ross Winthereik, 151–162. Durham, NC: Duke University Press, pp. 159–160.
records.text:
> I called my comparison between analogy-making practices in anthropology and analogy-making practices in magic a “meta-analogy.”
>
> — Graham M. Jones, "Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat," pp. 159–160

Both anthropologists and modern magicians compared “modern” and “primitive” magic. Comparing those two sets of comparisons, and diagramming them with the same base-target-concept triangle, showed Jones how experts in both fields reinforced a shared idea of disenchantment as distinctive of Western modernity, the argument of his book Magic's Reason. He notes that the method suits few projects, but it points to something general: the ways people categorize can themselves be compared and categorized.

records.title: The magic circle
records.description: A game takes place inside a boundary, in space or in agreement, where its own rules hold and ordinary life is set aside.
records.source: Johan Huizinga, Homo Ludens: A Study of the Play-Element in Culture (Dutch original 1938; English edition Roy Publishers, 1950; Beacon Press paperback, 1955), p. 10; Katie Salen and Eric Zimmerman, Rules of Play: Game Design Fundamentals (MIT Press, 2004 [2003]), pp. 95–96, as quoted in Jesper Juul, "The Magic Circle and the Puzzle Piece," in Stephan Günzel, Michael Liebe and Dieter Mersch, eds., Conference Proceedings of the Philosophy of Computer Games 2008 (Potsdam: University Press, 2008), pp. 56–67, p. 57; Eric Zimmerman, "Jerked Around by the Magic Circle: Clearing the Air Ten Years Later," Gamasutra, 2012.
records.text:
> The arena, the card-table, the magic circle, the temple, the stage, the screen, the tennis court, the court of justice, etc., are all in form and function play-grounds, i.e. forbidden spots, isolated, hedged round, hallowed, within which special rules obtain. All are temporary worlds within the ordinary world, dedicated to the performance of an act apart.
>
> — Johan Huizinga, *Homo Ludens*, p. 10

> In a very basic sense, the magic circle of a game is where the game takes place. To play a game means entering into a magic circle, or perhaps creating one as a game begins.
>
> — Katie Salen and Eric Zimmerman, Rules of Play (2004), pp. 95–96, as quoted in Jesper Juul, "The Magic Circle and the Puzzle Piece" (2008), p. 57

> The magic circle is the idea that a boundary exists between a game and the world outside the game.
>
> — Eric Zimmerman, "Jerked Around by the Magic Circle: Clearing the Air Ten Years Later" (2012), https://www.ericzimmerman.com/assets/pdfs/MCJ_Zimmerman.pdf

Huizinga used "magic circle" once in a list of set-apart places, the card table, the stage and the court of justice among them, where special rules hold for a while. Game designers Frank Lantz and Eric Zimmerman took up the phrase in their teaching around 1999, and Salen and Zimmerman's Rules of Play made it the standard name for the boundary around a game. Zimmerman later wrote that neither Huizinga nor Rules of Play claimed that games are completely separate from the rest of life. The circle is better understood as an agreement among players than as a wall.

See also: [huizinga](/cards/huizinga) · [salen zimmerman](/cards/salen-zimmerman)

records.title: Play (Huizinga's definition)
records.description: Play is a free activity, set apart from ordinary life in time and place, that follows fixed rules and absorbs the player completely.
records.source: Johan Huizinga, Homo Ludens: A Study of the Play-Element in Culture (Dutch original 1938; English edition Roy Publishers, 1950; Beacon Press paperback, 1955), pp. 8, 13.
records.text:
> Here, then, we have the first main characteristic of play: that it is free, is in fact freedom.
>
> — Johan Huizinga, *Homo Ludens*, p. 8

> Summing up the formal characteristics of play we might call it a free activity standing quite consciously outside "ordinary" life as being "not serious", but at the same time absorbing the player intensely and utterly. It is an activity connected with no material interest, and no profit can be gained by it.
